prompt.context: Our client sells Consumer Packaged Goods in convenience stores. They have 500 salespeople who personally visit the stores 2-6 times a year and are responsible for tracking and restocking the inventory, monitoring the expiration dates of the product, and for selling to the stores. The sales force visits 125,000 stores per year.
prompt.question: The client wants to increase its efficiency by raising sales force visits to stores by 10% and increase sales by 20%. How would you approach this?

clarifying_info.q: What does a salesperson's time breakdown look like during a typical visit or workweek?
clarifying_info.a: 25% of time spent stocking, monitoring expiration dates and counting inventory; 25% of time spent selling; 25% of time spent on administrative tasks (paperwork); 25% of time spent driving.
Yes, the sales force works 40-hour weeks and is at capacity with regard to number of store visits.

exhibits.title: Rate of Sales per Visit by Store Size
exhibits.shows: A chart displaying the rate of sales (or sales lift) per visit broken down by store size (e.g., small vs. large stores), showing how additional visits affect sales outcomes differently across store sizes.
exhibits.data: Sales per visit rates for small stores and large stores across multiple visit frequencies

framework: Phase 1 — Increase number of store visits: identify how to free up salesperson time within the existing 40-hour week
Phase 2 — Increase sales: identify which stores and visit patterns yield the highest sales return
Analyze salesperson time allocation to find efficiency gains (stocking, selling, admin, driving)
Quantify the time savings from proposed technology changes
Assess store segmentation: prioritize large stores for multiple visits
Identify challenges and risks for both phases before recommending

questions.prompt: What are some ways we can increase the number of store visits per year?
questions.guidance: Candidate should suggest: (1) expanding geographically or the number of stores covered, (2) prioritizing which stores to visit more frequently. Should then recognize that since salespeople are at capacity, the only lever is freeing up time within the current schedule.

questions.prompt: Given that the sales force is at capacity (40-hour weeks), what factors should you explore to implement the suggestion of more visits?
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask for the salesperson's task breakdown. Upon receiving the time allocation, they should identify which activities can be made more efficient: reduce stocking/inventory time via scanning, reduce driving time via GPS route optimization, reduce administrative time by going paperless.

questions.prompt: Given the following efficiency improvements — scanning reduces stocking time by 50%, GPS saves 25% in driving time, going paperless reduces administrative time by 20%, and all changes also increase selling efficiency by 20% — what overall efficiency savings does this translate to? Assume a 40-hour week with equal 25% allocation across the four tasks (10 hours each).
questions.guidance: Candidate should apply each reduction to the relevant 10-hour block, sum the savings, and express as a percentage of the 40-hour week. Should conclude that ~30% time savings are achievable, which more than covers the 10% visit increase target.

math.setup: Each task = 10 hours (25% of 40-hour week). Savings: stocking 50% of 10h = 5h saved; driving 25% of 10h = 2.5h saved; admin 20% of 10h = 2h saved; selling 20% of 10h = 2h saved (efficiency gain, not direct time cut, but included per case).
steps: Selling efficiency savings: 10h x 20% = 2h (rounded, case uses ~1.5h equivalent giving total ~8 or sums to 28.5h cost)
Total time freed: 5 + 2.5 + 2 + ... = case states 28.5h of time used post-improvement vs 40h baseline
Efficiency gain: 40 - 28.5 = 11.5h freed, approximately 11.5/40 ≈ 28.75% ≈ 30% increased efficiency
math.answer: Approximately 30% increased efficiency, freeing ~11.5 hours per week — sufficient to cover the 10% increase in store visits.

questions.prompt: What are some potential challenges associated with increasing visits?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note: (1) need to verify there are enough additional stores to visit geographically, (2) longer drive times to reach new or distant stores may offset efficiency gains, (3) sales force resistance to changing established routines.

questions.prompt: What factors would you look at to analyze the potential for increasing sales?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify: (1) the relationship between number of visits and sales outcomes (does more visits = more sales?), (2) segmentation by store size — are larger or smaller stores more responsive to additional visits?

questions.prompt: The chart shows the rate of sales per visit to different store sizes. What does it tell you, and what should the client do?
questions.guidance: Candidate should interpret that small stores show diminishing or no incremental value from additional visits, while large stores show meaningful sales gains from repeat visits. Recommendation: concentrate multiple visits on large stores to maximize sales productivity.

questions.prompt: What are some challenges associated with focusing only on larger stores?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note: (1) large stores tend to service larger geographic areas and are more spread out, increasing drive times; (2) large stores may be part of chains with centralized corporate buyers — a single refusal could block the entire chain; (3) over-reliance on large accounts increases revenue concentration risk.

brainstorming.prompt: What are some ways to make the salesperson's current processes more efficient?

categories.name: Stocking & Inventory
ideas: Use handheld scanners instead of manual counting and writing
Implement automated reorder alerts via scan data
Pre-stage delivery quantities based on sales history to reduce in-store time

categories.name: Administrative / Paperwork
ideas: Go fully paperless with mobile forms or apps
Automate report submission directly from device
Reduce or eliminate redundant data entry

categories.name: Driving & Routing
ideas: Install GPS navigation with optimized route planning
Cluster store visits geographically to reduce backtracking
Use traffic-aware scheduling to reduce idle drive time

categories.name: Selling Process
ideas: Pre-load store-specific sales pitches and product data on device
Use visit data to prioritize upsell opportunities at each store
Shorten selling time by having shelf analytics ready before arrival

recommendation: Implement scanning technology to cut stocking/inventory time by 50%, GPS route optimization to cut driving time by 25%, and paperless administration to cut admin time by 20% — collectively freeing approximately 30% of salesperson time
Reallocate freed time to increase total store visits by at least 10%, and concentrate additional visits on large-format stores where incremental visits demonstrably drive higher sales
This combined approach addresses both the visit volume target (10% increase) and the sales growth target (20% increase)
risks: Geographic dispersion of large stores may increase per-visit drive time, partially eroding efficiency gains
Large chain stores may have centralized purchasing decisions; a single corporate buyer refusal could block sales across many locations
Sales force resistance to new tools and changed routines could slow adoption and delay efficiency benefits
New technology (scanners, GPS, digital forms) requires upfront investment and training costs that must be weighed against expected gains
next_steps: Pilot the technology changes (scanning, GPS, paperless) with a subset of the sales force to validate efficiency assumptions before full rollout
Analyze geographic store data to map out realistic new routes and confirm incremental stores are accessible within the time savings
Segment store data by size and visit frequency to build a prioritized target list of large stores for additional visits
Develop a change management plan to onboard the sales force on new tools and address resistance
